<reason>CON chose a narrow-ground strategy: concede that every abusive sale (stalkers, priest, clinic lists, foreign buyers) must be banned regardless of consent, and stake the whole case on one exception—vetted public-interest planners accessing individual trajectories in a secure environment. PRO immediately exploited that concession, framed the remaining dispute as a single sympathetic planner versus the entire pipeline, and then won the weighing on it: when CON's rule fails (regulator misjudges a front), the harm is an irreversible trace; when PRO's rule fails, the harm is a thinner evacuation model that could be repaired with a plainly-worded prompt most people would accept. CON's best point—that PRO permits brokers' own nonconsensual aggregate analysis, so what marginal harm does the planner add—was real and PRO's "second custodian" answer was only partially satisfying. But CON undercut itself in A1 by admitting "no remedy can undo disclosure" and offering post-hoc compensation, which PRO's closing turned into the decisive line. PRO also handled CON's Q1 honestly (conceding the access counts as a sale) and adapted rather than dodged. CON's closing was competent but largely reasserted the inconsistency charge without showing why the exception's value outweighs the asymmetric failure cost. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1/A2 in Rebuttal 2 followed by its closing: conceding CON's secure-room access is a covered sale, then reframing CON's own safeguards as "fingerprints of a transaction everyone knows is dangerous," and finally quoting CON's admission that "no remedy can undo disclosure" to show consent places the halt before the irreversible step while CON's remedy arrives after.</best_rebuttal>
